questions.stem: Sort the materials into transparent, translucent or opaque.
questions.explanation: Transparent materials let almost all light through. Translucent materials let some through but scatter it. Opaque materials let none through.

questions.stem: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
questions.explanation: Cardboard is opaque, so it blocks all the light. Clear glass and water let light pass, and tracing paper lets some through.

questions.stem: Light travels in ___ lines. A shadow forms when an ___ object blocks the light.
questions.explanation: Light cannot bend round an opaque object, so a dark area, the shadow, is left behind it.

questions.stem: A shadow shows the colours of the object that makes it.
questions.explanation: A shadow shows only the outline shape of the object. It has no colour or detail.

questions.stem: Shadows point towards the Sun.
questions.explanation: The object blocks the light coming from the Sun, so the shadow falls on the side **away** from the Sun.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: lets some light through but scatters it
questions.explanation: These key words describe how materials treat light and how we measure how bright light is.

questions.stem: Why are shadows longer in the morning and evening than at midday?
options: The Sun is low in the sky.
The shadow is pushed by the wind.
questions.explanation: When the Sun is low, its light hits objects at a slant and makes long shadows. At midday the Sun is highest, so shadows are shortest.

questions.stem: Which of these show that light travels in straight lines? Choose all that are right.
options: Sunbeams shine through a gap in the curtains.
A torch beam cuts through mist.
We cannot see round a corner.
Light bends round a wall to fill its shadow.
questions.explanation: Beams, and not being able to see round corners, show straight-line travel. If light bent round objects there would be no shadows.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a shadow puppet’s shadow forms.
sequence: The light travels in straight lines.
The opaque puppet blocks some of the light.
A dark shape of the puppet appears on the cloth screen.
questions.explanation: Because the light cannot bend round or go through the puppet, the screen behind it stays dark in the shape of the puppet.

questions.stem: Why can you read a book through clear glass but not through tracing paper or cardboard?
questions.model_answer: Clear glass is transparent, so light passes straight through. Tracing paper is translucent and scatters the light so words look blurred. Cardboard is opaque and lets no light through.
questions.explanation: How clearly we see through a material depends on whether it lets light pass straight through, scatters it or blocks it.

questions.stem: What is the unit of light intensity?
questions.explanation: Light intensity (how bright light is) is measured with a light meter in lux.

questions.stem: Moving an object further from the torch makes its shadow smaller and sharper.
questions.explanation: A nearer object blocks more of the light and makes a bigger shadow. Moving it away makes the shadow smaller and sharper.

questions.stem: Why can you not see a clear shadow on a very cloudy day?
questions.model_answer: Clouds scatter the sunlight, so light comes from all directions and nothing blocks all of it.
questions.explanation: A clear shadow needs light from one direction that an object blocks. Clouds mix the light up so no dark area forms.

questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
questions.explanation: Light is very fast, about 300 000 km every second, but the Sun is so far away that its light still takes about 8 minutes to get here.

questions.stem: The picture shows a stick and its shadow at three times of day. When is the shadow shortest?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow at morning, midday and evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so the shadow is shortest. In the morning and evening it is long.

questions.stem: Look at the picture. The evening shadow is long because the Sun is low in the sky.
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow at morning, midday and evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: When the Sun is low, objects block its light at a slant and make long shadows. The morning shadow is long for the same reason.

questions.stem: In the picture the object is moved **closer to the torch**. What happens to the shadow on the screen?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
questions.explanation: A nearer object blocks more of the light from the torch, so its shadow is bigger (and a little more blurred).

questions.stem: Without changing the object in the picture, how could you make a different shadow **shape**?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
questions.explanation: The shadow is the outline of the object as seen from the light. Turning or tilting the object changes the outline, so the shape changes.

questions.stem: Why is there a dark shadow on the screen in the picture?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
options: The torch gives out dark light.
The screen absorbs all the light.
The object makes its own darkness.
The opaque object blocks the light.
questions.explanation: Light cannot go through an opaque object or bend round it, so the screen behind it receives no light.

questions.stem: Rafi is putting on a shadow puppet show with a lamp and a cloth screen. How can he make a puppet’s shadow bigger?
options: move it closer to the lamp
move it closer to the screen
move it further from the lamp
questions.explanation: The closer the puppet is to the lamp, the more light it blocks and the bigger the shadow. Colour makes no difference to a shadow.

questions.stem: A hot Dhaka classroom has glare near the windows and a dark back corner. Which ideas would help make it brighter and cooler? Choose all that are right.
options: paint the walls and ceiling white
use translucent blinds on the windows
questions.explanation: White surfaces reflect light round the room. Translucent blinds let light in but cut glare and heat. Trees block direct sun. Black walls and thick curtains make the room darker.

questions.stem: A light meter shows 120 lux at the back corner of a classroom. Experts recommend 300 to 500 lux for reading, so this corner is too dim.
questions.explanation: 120 lux is well below 300 lux. Too little light strains the eyes, so learners at the back may need more light or a better seat.

questions.stem: The school has a sundial. Why does its shadow move round during the day?
options: The stick slowly turns round on the ground.
The wind pushes the shadow round the stick.
The Sun gets bigger and then smaller.
The Sun seems to move as the Earth spins.
questions.explanation: Shadows always point away from the Sun. As the Sun seems to move from east to west, the shadow moves round, so the sundial can tell the time.

questions.stem: Joy wants a lampshade that gives soft light, not a harsh glare. Which material is best?
questions.explanation: Thin cotton cloth is translucent, so it lets some light through but scatters it. Steel and cardboard block it, and clear glass lets a harsh glare through.

questions.stem: Anika says one window gives more light than another. Measuring both with a light meter app is fairer than saying "it looks quite bright".
questions.explanation: A light meter gives a number in lux, so the results can be compared and checked by other people.

questions.stem: Nadia measured a 1 m stick’s shadow in the school yard (example data): 8 am 210 cm, 10 am 80 cm, 12 noon 30 cm, 2 pm 75 cm, 4 pm 190 cm. Which conclusions are supported? Choose all that are right.
options: The shadow was shortest at 12 noon.
The 8 am shadow was more than twice as long as the 10 am shadow.
The shadows at 10 am and 2 pm were exactly the same length.
The shadow got longer between 2 pm and 4 pm.
questions.explanation: 30 cm is the smallest. 210 ÷ 80 is about 2.6, so more than double. 80 cm and 75 cm are close but not equal, and the test did not compare different sticks.

questions.stem: Jamal held a 10 cm puppet at different distances from a torch, with a screen 60 cm away (example data): 10 cm → shadow 60 cm; 20 cm → 30 cm; 30 cm → 20 cm; 40 cm → 15 cm; 50 cm → 12 cm. Predict the shadow height with the puppet 15 cm from the torch: about ___ cm.
questions.explanation: The closer the puppet, the taller the shadow. Distance × shadow height is always 600 (10 × 60, 20 × 30, 30 × 20…), so at 15 cm the shadow is 600 ÷ 15 = 40 cm.

questions.stem: In Jamal’s test, which change would make the test unfair?
options: using the same torch every time
using a bigger puppet for the 30 cm trial
keeping the screen 60 cm from the torch
measuring the shadow height each time
questions.explanation: Only the distance from the torch may change. A different puppet size would change the shadow too, so we could not tell what caused the difference.

questions.stem: In 1676 Ole Rømer noticed that one of Jupiter’s moons appeared from behind the planet later than expected when Earth was further away. What did this show about light?
questions.model_answer: Light takes time to travel. When Earth was further away, the light had further to go, so it arrived later.
questions.explanation: People once thought light arrived instantly. Rømer’s observation showed that light has a speed, so a longer distance means a longer travel time.

questions.stem: A well-lit classroom has 300 to 500 lux. A sunny day outdoors has 50 000 to 100 000 lux. At the very least, how many times brighter is a sunny day than the brightest well-lit classroom?
questions.explanation: Compare the lowest sunny value with the highest classroom value: 50 000 ÷ 500 = 100. So a sunny day is at least 100 times brighter.
